nameStory: The Callery pear gets its name from Joseph-Marie Callery, a French missionary who collected plants in China in the 1800s and sent specimens back to Europe. This tree is native to East Asia, so unlike our native American pears, it carries the name of its European 'discoverer' rather than reflecting any connection to New England.
description: Callery pear is a medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 30-50 feet tall with a distinctive oval to pyramid shape when young. It's most famous for its abundant white spring flowers that bloom before the leaves emerge, creating spectacular displays along roadsides and in suburban landscapes. The tree has glossy, oval leaves that turn brilliant orange-red in fall, and produces small, hard fruits that birds love but humans find inedible. Many people know this tree by its most common cultivar name, Bradford pear.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense clusters of white flowers with 5 rounded petals bloom in early spring before leaves appear, but beware - they smell terrible, like rotting fish or ammonia, especially on warm days

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy, oval to heart-shaped leaves with finely toothed edges, arranged alternately on branches and feeling smooth and waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round, brownish fruits about the size of a large pea, hard and gritty with a dry, chalky texture - very different from juicy eating pears

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark when young that develops shallow furrows and a slightly scaly texture with age, never becoming deeply ridged

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Distinctive upright oval shape when young, though older trees often develop weak branch angles that make them prone to splitting in storms

habitat: Callery pear thrives in disturbed areas, roadsides, abandoned lots, and forest edges throughout New England's lower elevations. Originally planted as ornamental street trees and in suburban landscapes, it has escaped cultivation and now grows wild in many areas. It tolerates poor soils, pollution, and urban conditions better than most trees.

seasonality.spring: The tree explodes with white flowers in April before leaves emerge, creating the year's most obvious identification opportunity - just follow your nose to the fishy smell.
seasonality.summer: Glossy green leaves create dense shade, and small fruits begin developing, though they're not very noticeable until later in the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant orange to red, making it one of the showiest fall color trees, while small brown fruits become more visible and attract birds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's characteristic oval shape, and persistent small fruits often remain attached, providing food for wildlife through the cold months.

funFact: Bradford pear trees were once hailed as the perfect street tree because they were supposed to be sterile and not produce messy fruit - but nature found a way! When different cultivars are planted near each other, they can cross-pollinate and create fertile offspring that are now spreading into wild areas and considered invasive in many states.
confusionNotes: The white spring flowers might be confused with native serviceberry or wild cherry, but the awful fishy smell of Callery pear flowers is unmistakable - if it smells bad, it's definitely Callery pear. Native fruit trees have pleasant or no flower fragrance.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a pear, Callery pears are completely different from the sweet, juicy pears we eat, which come from a different species (Pyrus communis). The 'Bradford' cultivar became so popular in landscaping that many people call all Callery pears 'Bradford pears,' but Bradford is actually just one of many cultivated varieties of this Asian species.
compareHints: Callery pear differs from common eating pear trees by its much smaller, hard, inedible fruits and terrible-smelling flowers. Common pear trees produce large, soft, sweet fruits and have pleasantly fragrant white flowers. Callery pear also tends to have a more upright, formal growth habit compared to the more spreading shape of traditional pear trees.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common pear differs from its invasive cousin, Callery pear, by having much larger, edible fruits and flowers that appear before the leaves rather than with them.
